quote: The surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.
firstReading: Paul identifies the true circumcision not by bodily ancestry or religious achievement, but by worship offered in the Spirit of God, glorying in Christ Jesus, and refusing confidence in the flesh. Though Paul once possessed impressive Jewish credentials and zeal, he now judges every former ground for boasting as loss when set beside the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus.
psalmSummary: The psalm summons God’s people to sing to the Lord, speak of his wonders, and rejoice in his holy name. They are to seek the Lord and his strength continually, remembering the mighty deeds he has done. As descendants of Abraham and children of Jacob, they belong to the God whose judgments reach throughout the earth and whose covenantal faithfulness endures.
gospelSummary: Jesus receives tax collectors and sinners who draw near to hear him, provoking criticism from Pharisees and scribes. In response, he tells of a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to seek one that is lost, then rejoices with his friends when it is found. He follows with the image of a woman diligently searching for one lost coin and calling others to rejoice when she finds it. Jesus reveals that heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents more than over those who imagine themselves secure and without need of repentance. God’s mercy actively seeks the lost and restores them to communion.
saintReflection: Saints Domninus, Theotimus, and Companions (Commemoration): Saints Domninus, Theotimus, and their companions are remembered among the Christians who suffered during the persecution associated with Emperor Diocletian. Eusebius of Caesarea preserves testimony to believers in Palestine who endured execution, imprisonment, forced labor, and mutilation rather than deny Christ. The surviving accounts concern several witnesses and must be received without embellishing uncertain details, yet the center of their commemoration is clear: baptismal fidelity remained stronger than imperial coercion. Their martyrdom does not glorify violence or contempt for life; it confesses that the risen Lord alone has final authority over life and death. These martyrs call the Church to pray for the persecuted, to resist every assault upon conscience and human dignity, and to forgive enemies while remaining steadfast in the truth.
dailyPrayer:
Lord Jesus Christ, you came to seek and save those who were lost. Draw near to all who are burdened by sin, fear, loneliness, persecution, or the memory of grievous wounds. Grant us the humility to confess that our hope does not rest in ancestry, accomplishments, discipline, or any work of the flesh, but in your mercy and in the gift of knowing you.

Teach us to seek the Father with persevering hearts and to remember his mighty deeds. Make your Church rejoice not in judgment over sinners, but in every return to your communion. Give courage to Christians who suffer for your name, especially those whose conscience, dignity, or freedom to worship is attacked. Through the intercession of Saints Domninus, Theotimus, and their companions, make us steadfast in baptismal faith, gentle toward enemies, and faithful in truth. May the joy of heaven over repentance shape our prayer, our repentance, and our welcome of every person you call home. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
Today’s Scriptures unite conversion with the mystery of grace. Paul does not despise God’s gifts to Israel or deny the value of his former life; rather, he refuses to make any created privilege the basis of righteousness before God. The Christian’s confidence is Christ himself, known in faith and worshiped in the Holy Spirit. This is the interior meaning of belonging to the true people of God.

Luke discloses the heart of the God whom Paul serves. God does not merely permit the sinner’s return; he seeks, finds, restores, and rejoices. Repentance is therefore not a transaction by which a person earns acceptance. It is the grace-enabled turning of the lost toward the One who has already come in search of them. The martyrs witnessed to this same lordship of Christ. Their fidelity arose from baptismal belonging: no earthly power could claim the worship and obedience owed to the risen Lord. The Church joins their steadfast confession to humble repentance, confident that divine mercy gathers the lost into communion.
exegesis:
Context: Philippians 3:3-8 and Luke 15:1-10 confront two opposite but related spiritual dangers: confidence in oneself and despair over one’s lostness. Paul writes as one who knew the religious privileges of Israel from within. He lists his circumcision, ancestry, observance of the Law, zeal, and outward righteousness, not to ridicule these realities, but to show that none can become a claim upon God. Jesus, meanwhile, is criticized precisely because he receives those whom others judge unworthy. The readings reveal that communion with God rests neither on human status nor on exclusion of the sinful, but on Christ’s gracious initiative and the repentant response it awakens.

First Reading: Paul calls believers the true circumcision because their identity is centered on worship in the Spirit of God, glory in Christ Jesus, and renunciation of confidence in the flesh. Flesh here does not mean the goodness of the created body; it means human existence considered as though it could establish itself before God by its own resources. Paul had abundant reasons for such confidence according to the standards of his former life. Yet the encounter with Christ reordered every value. What once appeared gain is counted loss beside knowing the crucified and risen Lord. Christian faith does not add Christ as an ornament to self-justification. It receives Christ as the one treasure by whom every other gift finds its proper place.

Psalm: Psalm 105 answers Paul’s teaching with the language of worship and memory. Israel is summoned to sing, seek the Lord’s strength, and remember his marvelous works. This remembrance guards the community from imagining that it created its own identity. Abraham’s descendants and Jacob’s children exist because God called, guided, judged, and kept covenant. The psalm’s invitation to seek the Lord continually is not a search for an absent deity, but a persevering return to the God who has already made himself known in saving deeds. For Christians, this prayer becomes fully Christological: the Father’s covenantal faithfulness is displayed definitively in the Son, through whom sinners are brought into the worship of God.

Gospel: The setting in Luke is essential. Tax collectors and sinners approach Jesus in order to hear him. Their nearness is itself a sign of grace, but it provokes the murmuring of Pharisees and scribes. Jesus does not answer with an abstract defense. He tells parables in which loss causes a search and recovery brings communal joy. The shepherd seeks the single sheep; the woman carefully searches for the lost coin. The images emphasize divine initiative. The sheep does not locate the shepherd, and the coin cannot contribute to its recovery. God’s mercy precedes and enables repentance, while never treating the sinner’s conversion as unimportant. Heaven rejoices when the lost person turns back because restored communion is the purpose of the search.

Gospel: Jesus’ reference to those who have no need of repentance exposes the peril of presumed righteousness. It cannot mean that some human beings truly stand before God without need of conversion. Rather, it addresses those who believe themselves secure enough to look on others without mercy. The Pharisees and scribes are invited to enter the joy of God, not merely to tolerate Jesus’ welcome. Their complaint places distance between themselves and the divine rejoicing revealed in Christ. The parables therefore summon every hearer to two conversions: the lost must receive the mercy that seeks them, and the apparently secure must rejoice when mercy restores another. The Church is faithful to her Lord when her proclamation of truth is joined to his compassion for sinners.

Saints: Saints Domninus, Theotimus, and their companions bear witness to the same primacy of Christ proclaimed by Paul. The surviving testimony concerning Christians in Palestine during the persecution associated with Diocletian must not be enlarged with uncertain details. What their commemoration securely confesses is baptismal fidelity under coercion. They did not treat earthly authority as ultimate, because the risen Lord has final authority over life and death. Their witness must never be used to praise suffering for its own sake or to foster hatred toward persecutors. Christian martyrdom is an act of worship, a refusal to deny Christ, and a testimony that human dignity and conscience belong to God. Their steadfastness calls believers to intercede for persecuted Christians and to forgive enemies without surrendering the truth.

Today: The readings invite a concrete ecclesial examination of heart. Do we rest our hope in Christ, or do we quietly rely on achievements, reputation, lineage, or outward religious correctness? Do we seek the Lord by recalling his mercy, or do we use religious knowledge to separate ourselves from those in need of conversion? The shepherd’s search and the woman’s careful diligence reveal how precious each person is to God. Therefore, prayer for repentance must include prayer that the Church may welcome those whom Christ draws near. In a world where conscience can be pressured and discipleship can carry a cost, the martyrs also teach calm courage. Knowing Christ surpasses every lesser claim, and the joy of heaven gives believers strength to remain faithful and merciful.
